item.title: 'I worked so hard' - Vatuwaqa resident loses home and vehicles in fire
item.description: It was not a good Sunday for Timoci Nadukeva, whose home was destroyed in a fire at Muanivatu Settlement in Vatuwaqa this morning. Nadukeva says he was at the Waila Market when a friend informed him that his house was on fire.
item.content:encoded:
It was not a good Sunday for Timoci Nadukeva, whose home was destroyed in a fire at Muanivatu Settlement in Vatuwaqa this morning.

Nadukeva says he was at the Waila Market when a friend informed him that his house was on fire.

He says he initially did not believe his friend, but soon realised he was serious.

When he arrived home, he found the house engulfed in flames.

Nadukeva says his child was home alone when the fire broke out a nd noticed that the fire had started in the mother's room before running out of the house.

He is grateful that no one was injured, especially his child.

However, the fire destroyed all their belongings, including his two vehicles.

Nadukeva says he has worked so hard to build what he had, only to lose it all in the fire.

He says he does not know what he will do next and is appealing to the Government to assist him and his family.

The cause of the fire is yet to be determined, and firefighters are at the scene.

We have sent questions to the National Fire Authority.

item.title: Chaudhry says religion and State must remain separate
item.description: Former Prime Minister Mahendra Chaudhry says religion and the State must remain separate to protect Fiji's multiracial society from division, stressing that all people should be free to practise their faith without the government favouring one religion over another. Making his submission during the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026 public consultation in Labasa, Chaudhry says he has no problem with
item.content:encoded:
Former Prime Minister Mahendra Chaudhry says religion and the State must remain separate to protect Fiji's multiracial society from division, stressing that all people should be free to practise their faith without the government favouring one religion over another.

Making his submission during the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026 public consultation in Labasa, Chaudhry says he has no problem with Christian values but believes religion and the State must remain separate.

Chaudhry says Fiji is a multiracial country, and introducing provisions that could favour one religion could create serious divisions between different communities.

Insert: Chaudhry says religion and state must remain separate 25th Oct 26 PT

He questions why religious provisions that have generated controversy should be included in the proposed Constitution when people are already allowed to practise their faith freely.

Chaudhry urges the committee to seriously consider this issue.

He also raises concerns about the overall direction of the Constitution Amendment Bill 32 of 2026, describing it as divisive, undemocratic and discriminatory in several of its provisions.

Chaudhry says Fiji should focus more on addressing the pressing problems facing the country rather than rushing to introduce another Constitution.

He says the country is dealing with poverty, hunger, unemployment, poor health services, challenges in education, crumbling infrastructure, drug trafficking, HIV and non-communicable diseases.

Chaudhry says the economy must be a priority because a strong economy is necessary for the Government to deliver better services and opportunities to the people.

He questions whether previous constitutions have adequately served the people, saying Fiji is worse off today than it was at independence in several respects.

Chaudhry also questions why the constitutional review process is being rushed, saying Fiji can hold its next general elections under the existing Constitution and allow the incoming government to address constitutional reform through proper and thorough public consultation.

He says people participating in the consultations have repeatedly called for more time, with many saying they have barely had an opportunity to examine the proposed Constitution.

Chaudhry says his submissions to the Constitution Review Commission, which he presented on 7th July, still stand.

He says the Constitution Amendment Bill 32 being considered by Parliament differs significantly from the draft prepared by the Constitution Review Commission and presented to Parliament on 22nd September.

He believes the committee should be considering the draft prepared by the Commission under the President's mandate.

Chaudhry also raises concerns about the transitional provisions in clauses 211, 219 and 221 of the proposed Constitution.

He says these provisions create suspicion that they could allow existing Members of Parliament to continue into a new government under the new Constitution without a general election.

He calls for clarification on why these clauses have been included if the intention is to hold elections.

Chaudhry also questions the proposed referendum and election timetable, pointing to the planned referendum on 9th December, with results expected by 14th December, and the 24th December deadline for issuing the writ of elections.

He says the timing, when considered alongside the transitional provisions, raises concerns that must be addressed.

On minority rights, Chaudhry says communities that make up approximately 38 percent of Fiji's population need stronger assurances about their future, particularly regarding access to land and economic opportunities.

He says the indigenous iTaukei people own roughly 90 to 92 percent of Fiji's land, leaving limited freehold and State land available for housing, agriculture and commercial purposes.

Chaudhry says people have been displaced from farms and businesses when leases expire and are not renewed, and he believes greater certainty is needed for those affected.

He also highlights the lack of development in rural areas, saying some Indigenous iTaukei people working in Australia and New Zealand want to remain overseas because of limited opportunities and a lack of reliable income in their communities.

Chaudhry says productive land, including land previously used for sugarcane farming, is increasingly being left unused and becoming overgrown.

He warns that failing to address these issues could widen economic disparities between communities and says greater investment in rural development is needed.

Chaudhry says these important national issues require longer discussions and meaningful dialogue, which he believes have been missing from the current process.

He clarifies that he is not opposed to amending the 2013 Constitution, saying some provisions should be reviewed to ensure they comply with democratic norms and international treaties, instruments and conventions to which Fiji is a party.

However, he stresses that any constitutional changes must be made through a democratic, inclusive, transparent and lawfully mandated process, with sufficient time for people to understand the proposals and have their voices heard.

item.title: Man allegedly found with methamphetamine, marijuana and $2,121
item.description: A 33-year-old man from Cunningham, Suva, was allegedly found with methamphetamine, marijuana and $2,121.20 believed to be proceeds of crime during a police search last night. Police say the man was arrested after officers conducting routine patrols in the Cunningham area searched him.
item.content:encoded:
A 33-year-old man from Cunningham, Suva, was allegedly found with methamphetamine, marijuana and $2,121.20 believed to be proceeds of crime during a police search last night.

Police say the man was arrested after officers conducting routine patrols in the Cunningham area searched him.

He was allegedly found with a clear plastic bag containing a white crystalline substance believed to be methamphetamine and dried leaves believed to be marijuana.

Police say the $2,121.20 found in his possession is believed to be proceeds of crime.

item.title: Coalition lacked numbers to amend Constitution in 2022, Balawa questions SODELPA’s opposition to Bill
item.description: The Coalition Government did not have enough parliamentary votes to amend the 2013 Constitution after the 2022 general elections, with People’s Alliance General Secretary Sila Balawa saying it had only 29 MPs against the required 42 votes under the original 75 percent threshold. Balawa says this is an important factor to consider when questioning why the Coalition Government did not amend the Cons
item.content:encoded:
The Coalition Government did not have enough parliamentary votes to amend the 2013 Constitution after the 2022 general elections, with People’s Alliance General Secretary Sila Balawa saying it had only 29 MPs against the required 42 votes under the original 75 percent threshold.

Balawa says this is an important factor to consider when questioning why the Coalition Government did not amend the Constitution within its first 100 days or first two years in office.

He says following the 2022 general elections, Parliament had 55 seats, with FijiFirst holding 26, the People’s Alliance 21, the National Federation Party 5 and SODELPA 3.

The Coalition Government was formed with 29 MPs, giving it a narrow majority over FijiFirst’s 26 MPs.

However, under the original 2013 Constitution, constitutional amendments required a 75 percent parliamentary majority, meaning at least 42 votes out of 55.

Balawa questions where the Government was expected to find the additional 13 votes during its first 100 days.

He says the parliamentary situation changed after FijiFirst was deregistered in July 2024, when its 26 MPs became Independents.

In January 2025, nine former FijiFirst MPs, known as the G9, joined the Government, increasing its parliamentary strength from 29 to 38 MPs.

In March 2025, two more former FijiFirst MPs, Sachida Nand and Shalen Kumar, joined the group, bringing the number of Independents supporting the Government to 11, known as the G11.

Despite these changes, Balawa says the original three-quarters threshold remained a major obstacle to constitutional amendments.

He says the legal position changed on 29th August 2025, when the Supreme Court clarified that constitutional amendments require the support of at least two-thirds of all Members of Parliament at the second and third readings, rather than the previous three-quarters requirement.

Balawa says this created a legal pathway for constitutional reform.

According to Balawa, the Speaker’s ruling in October 2026 requires 35 votes if all 53 MPs occupying parliamentary seats are present and seated.

He says the People’s Alliance has 20 MPs, the NFP has 4 and the G11 Independents have 11, giving them a combined total of 35 votes without the support of SODELPA’s three MPs, provided all those members support the Bill.

However, Balawa questions SODELPA’s decision not to support the Constitution Amendment Bill 2026 in its current form.

He says SODELPA campaigned during the 2014, 2018 and 2022 general elections on protecting iTaukei interests and opposing the 2013 Constitution.

He also points to the Coalition Agreement, which committed the Government to reviewing the Constitution and considering amendments.

Balawa questions why SODELPA would campaign for constitutional change over three general elections but withhold its support when the opportunity to make changes is now available.

He acknowledges that SODELPA has every right to scrutinise Bill 32 but says the party has a responsibility to explain to its supporters why it will not support the Bill in its current form.

Balawa argues that the Government should not be blamed for failing to amend the Constitution when it did not have the necessary parliamentary numbers, only for the process to be opposed now that the numbers and legal pathway are available.

He says the key question is whether SODELPA still stands by the commitments it made to voters in 2014, 2018 and 2022.
